metadata.note: The Eastern Railroad and the Portland, Saco and Portsmouth Railroad, the two companies whose 1842 connection at South Berwick, ME gave Boston and Portland their first direct passenger rail link -- researched from Wikipedia and railroad-history sites in response to a question about when that first connection happened. This dataset previously only covered the streamliner-era Flying Yankee (1935 onward, see data/boston_and_maine_flying_yankee.geojson), not the corridor's actual 1838-1935 origin. The Eastern Railroad built north from Boston in stages (Salem 1838, Ipswich 1839, Newburyport and the NH line 1840, on to Portsmouth soon after) while the Portland, Saco and Portsmouth Railroad built south from Portland, and the two met at South Berwick in 1842. Both were absorbed by the Boston & Maine Railroad (the Eastern Railroad leased Dec 23 1883, with full absorption of its assets including the PS&P by 1884), which ran the corridor as its Eastern Division until the Flying Yankee streamliner took over the route's flagship service in 1935. GEOMETRY UPGRADED 2026-08-24: replaced the original handful of hand-placed waypoints with real-traced OpenStreetMap track geometry (Overpass API, shortest-path graph search). North Station-Salem-Newburyport and Scarborough-Saco-Biddeford-Kennebunk-South Berwick both resolved to connected, plausible real track. Two stretches did NOT resolve to plausible connected paths and remain straight-line approximations, flagged honestly: Newburyport-Portsmouth (~31km) has no connected active/abandoned rail tagging at all in OSM for this stretch -- the modern MBTA Newburyport/Rockport Line dead-ends at Newburyport and does not continue into New Hampshire, and the original Eastern Railroad's coastal alignment through Salisbury/Seabrook/Hampton appears to have no surviving traced remnant; and Portland-Scarborough, where OSM's active rail tagging does connect but only via an implausible ~35km detour (vs. 9.7km straight-line) through Portland's rail yards, so a straight line was used instead of that unrealistic path. Note this coastal alignment is a genuinely different physical route from the modern Amtrak Downeaster (which runs inland via Haverhill-Exeter-Dover), so it could not simply reuse that GTFS geometry the way the Flying Yankee file does. Era boundaries follow real corporate-history milestones (line openings, mergers); headway_min and avg_speed_kmh within each era are estimates, not sourced from real timetables.
metadata.source: Wikipedia (Eastern Railroad, Portland Saco and Portsmouth Railroad), easterntrail.org, american-rails.com, nashuacitystation.org (see conversation for citations)
geometry_sources: OpenStreetMap (via Overpass API, overpass.openstreetmap.fr mirror): railway=rail (active) combined with railway=abandoned/disused tagging, Boston to Portland via the coastal alignment; routed via Dijkstra shortest path between each station's geocoded coordinates. Newburyport-Portsmouth (no connected tagging) and Portland-Scarborough (implausible-detour check triggered) are straight-line fallbacks.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
